item.title: Friendkeeping and the Work of Sustaining Adult Friendships
item.description:
Friends

Friendkeeping and the Work of Sustaining Adult Friendships

Who will step forward to help keep a friendship going?

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Friendkeepers step up to sustain adult friendships, much like kinkeepers in families.
  • The friendkeeper role involves organizing, sharing news, and mobilizing support within groups.
  • Building friendship networks before crises makes future support and coordination more effective.

No matter what life stage you are in, it is worth considering the well-being of your friendships. In my own case, I have lived in eight different U.S. states and moved across country several times, including as I retired. Most people regard friends as part of our convoy of life, much like long-haul truckers or ships that travel together. Some members of our life convoy are there for the length of our lifespan, others join in periodically, and others may exit.

Each of us makes choices about maintaining friendships and support boundaries (Johnson, 2025). My observation is that some people seem to find it easier to let friendships lapse, especially when we change jobs, move, graduate, find a new church or sports team, join new families, or see friends move on. Others find a way to sustain friendships beyond those times when we have regular contact. It certainly has become easier to maintain and renew friendships via digital and social media. However, most people will have times they need additional support or to hook into a local friendship community.

I have thought about and studied the role of people who are called family kinkeepers (Braithwaite et al., 2017; Rosenthal, 1985). These are people who “help enable and assist family communication. Kinkeepers plan family gatherings or help the family keep in touch with one another by providing updates on issues such as graduations, birth of a baby, or publicizing support needs if a family member becomes unemployed or is having surgery” (Braithwaite, 2022). My research teams have studied how people who play this kinkeeper role communicate and what they do and say to help families stay connected.

The Friendkeeper Role

The relationship “keeper” role is not just relevant to families. Gallagher and Gerstel (1993) pointed to what they called “friendkeeping,” which refers to a role dedicated to building and maintaining friendships. For many people, friendships may be as important, or even more important, than blood and legal families to provide help and social support. This can range from visits, transportation, errands, in-person care, accompanying to medical appointments, raising funds, organizing meals—any number of actions. Other important types of social support involve finding and sharing information and advice, encouraging emotional solidarity, and connecting a person to other support networks. Friendkeepers may provide the support themselves or help organize a response from among the friendship group.

Work of the Friendkeeper

Initiative

In many cases, someone needs to step forward as the friendkeeper of a particular pair or group. I have often functioned in the friendkeeper role, for example in recent years, for one of my college musical groups, faculty and students from my doctoral program, a small group of high school friends who live nearby, and a larger group of people who were members of a former church. Like kinkeepers, friendkeepers tend to step forward and undertake the role, rather than being assigned or voted in. What we learned with family kinkeepers is that they recognize they are playing the role and others look to them and identify them as kinkeepers. The same appears to be true for friendkeepers.

article continues after advertisement

If you want to see a friendship pair or group continue over time, you may want to consider stepping forward as a friendkeeper and do the work, such as sharing information, assistance, planning events, etc., whatever it takes to maintain friendships and meet needs. Or you may certainly encourage another person in that role or plan for rotating responsibilities. Some people express frustration with always being expected to take the lead (it can be a burden as well as a joy) and balance that frustration against the cost of letting friendship relationships lapse.

Organizing

The organizing role of friendkeepers can be broad. It is important to do what will benefit members of the friendship group, looking for what is needed to keep relationships together if that is the goal. Don’t be afraid to step forward and ask friendship group members to describe what they’d like to see.

Tasks can include managing communication, for example, creating and keeping a contact list, social media site, or newsletter, or sending notes, gifts, or other messages of encouragement. Friendkeepers are usually instrumental in organizing regular events like a holiday celebration or monthly outing, or one-time events, trips, or reunions.

Friendkeepers and members of the friendship group may benefit from seeking help with organizing. This is also a way to increase interest and commitment of the friendship group. Friendkeepers are likely in the best position to hear when friends have news or needs (e.g., lost a job, experiencing illness, birth of a child, loneliness). They can get the word out and provide or coordinate a response.

Challenges of the Friendkeeping Role

Friendkeeping roles are not without challenges. I discuss three here.

Accepting Friend Support

One potential difficulty is that some people may not be used to, or willing to, open themselves up for significant help from friends over family. That works if they have realistic expectations and experience of their family coming through. However, people who live far from family or do not have close family ties may not be able to depend on family to step forward in times of need. In these cases, support from friends may be a learned behavior. The more success a friendship pair or group experiences providing support to one another, the more their track record of support will help them going forward.

article continues after advertisement

Privacy

A second challenge is dealing with expectations of privacy. As friendkeepers often manage personal information, they need to consider who is included. If they manage the group's contact list, they need to be careful how it is used. For instance, I ran into a complication with friendkeeping when one member did not agree with how another person had presented a new name on the contact list and wanted changes.

The friendkeeper must thoughtfully consider what information is acceptable to share. I developed my own rule not to share information before checking with the person(s) whose needs I am hoping to address or with their closest relational partner if they are unable to communicate directly.

Place of the Family

A third challenge to friendkeeping is how the bio-legal families may react to close friendship relationships that may augment or replace families at some point. Family members may feel embarrassed or resentful when friends step in to help. Friendkeepers can easily find themselves caught in the middle between people who need support, their family, and the friendship group.

Friendkeeping Over the Years

We know that building and keeping friendship ties over the years can be challenging. However, friendship represents efforts worth making as it is difficult, if not impossible, to build support networks in an emergency, or in later life when friends may be experiencing limitations and health issues.

The friendkeeper role has the potential to be helpful in building and maintaining friendship networks, and having people prepared and able to step up when the unexpected happens. People will know who to call to get the ball rolling. This does not mean that the friendkeeper is solely responsible for providing all the support, but in the best of circumstances, they can communicate, get the word out, and help coordinate support when the need arises.

item.title: Is It a Behavioral Peculiarity or Psychiatric Disorder?
item.description:
Authenticity

Is It a Behavioral Peculiarity or Psychiatric Disorder?

If someone refers to you as “weird,” they might be paying you a compliment.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Eccentricity is not listed as a mental disorder in psychiatric manuals.
  • The eccentric’s brain usually functions well, just in a peculiar way.
  • Distress and social dysfunction, not just odd behavior, define true psychiatric disorders.

Most of us are inveterate people labelers. Introduce us to a new person, and the labeling commences: What category—niche—best describes them? Are they extroverted? Are they easy conversationalists and relaxation-inducing? Or do they come across as overly reserved, laconic, inept practitioners of the art of small talk? And if their general “vibe” is an especially negative one, what psychiatric diagnoses might best fit them?

Of course, in an era of relaxed social and cultural expectations, one has to be cautious about negatively labeling anyone. Psychiatrists and psychologists aren’t exempted from this caution. In fact, as a general rule, the more familiar one is with the fine points of the DSM, the more likely and frequent the tendency to describe people in psychiatric terms.

One popular tack is to attach a mental health label to the most extreme personalities and accept all lesser personality variations as “normal.” Although this is one option, it makes it that much harder to answer a key question: At what point does a behavioral peculiarity become a psychiatric disorder?

Take Joshua Abraham Norton, who appointed himself emperor of the United States by an edict he published in the San Francisco Bulletin on September 17, 1859. Along with disbanding both Democratic and Republican parties, Norton printed his own currency, which came to be accepted in many shops and restaurants in San Francisco. For over 20 years he patrolled the city sidewalks in the interest of seeing to it that they remained unobstructed. In the course of these perambulations, Emperor Norton dressed himself in a blue military uniform with golden epaulettes, along with a tall plumed beaver hat, a sword, and a rosette.

When Morton died in 1880, the San Francisco Chronicle headlined his passing as “Le Roi Est Mort.” All flags in the city were flown at half-mast, and 30,000 mourners were in attendance at a lavish graveside service.

While most American psychiatrists today would unhesitatingly label Morton as suffering from a psychotic delusion, the clinical psychologist David Weeks suggests that Norton was not psychotic or delusional at all, but a classic example of an eccentric.

As Weeks noted, the diagnosis of eccentricity was almost unknown when he began his training at Edinburgh in 1984, and “actual scientific knowledge about eccentrics was virtually non-existent. Further, eccentricity is taken on by free choice and is something positive and pleasurable to the individual.” It’s also clear, Weeks claims, that eccentricity and psychosis are not the same thing. “The psychotic state severely disrupts thought processes, leaving the person dysfunctional, whereas the eccentric’s brain usually functions perfectly well—it just does so in peculiar and largely unknown (but not unknowable) ways.”

Eccentricity can involve a panoply of unusual beliefs and behaviors: odd preoccupations, unusual speech, mannerisms or interests; disregard for day-to-day niceties; unconventional dress or appearance; and an intense focused interest in intellectual, artistic, or scientific topics. How does this differ from interests and behaviors based on a psychiatric disorder?

article continues after advertisement

In almost all instances, mental illness is accompanied by internal distress and behaviors that seriously interfere with normal relationships and social functioning. In short, a designation of mental illness can never be based solely on what is deemed unusual behavior (largely a social rather than a psychiatric construct), but must always involve one or more significant disturbances in cognition, emotional control, or behavioral organization.

If eccentricity does evolve into mental illness, it does so in distinct progressive stages: eccentric, increasingly eccentric, and maximally eccentric. Only the extremes of eccentricity may represent a definite psychosis.

Currently, neither the DSM nor the World Health Organization ICD-11 lists the diagnosis of eccentric disorder or eccentric personality. In other words, two of the main psychiatric diagnostic manuals don’t list eccentric behavior as a mental health issue. British psychiatrists in particular remain open to the concept that eccentricity is an extreme of normal personality rather than an indication of psychopathology. Nor should this come as a surprise.

British culture historically showed more tolerance than our own for eccentricity, which is often regarded with wry amusement. In addition, British cultural stereotypes of eccentricity were well established long before psychiatrists on either side of the “pond” made the case that eccentricity was or was not a form of mental illness. Think of Dickens, whose works contain a human menagerie of eccentric characters. Dickens’ depictions of British eccentrics were based on social, rather than medical, observations and were often treated as fascinating, amusing, and even celebratory (shades of Emperor Norton). Or consider the essayist and dictionary kingpin Samuel Johnson, who exhibited a cornucopia of odd mannerisms, tics, and distinctly unorthodox mental preoccupations. Rather than arousing concern or uneasiness among his friends and acquaintances, Johnson’s personal eccentricities were accepted as harmless traits in an amusing though puzzling personage.

article continues after advertisement

According to recent research, eccentricity isn’t always a negative personality dimension. If you substitute the word “weird” for eccentric, you include some of the most productive and creative figures in the 21st century, such as Elon Musk, Tony Hsieh, and the late Steve Jobs.

During his tenure at Zappos, Hsieh was notorious for asking job applicants how weird they were on a scale of 1 to 10. According to Jun-Yeob Kim, an assistant professor at the Department of Management at the University of Central Florida, who maintains a keen interest in weirdness, “Consistent with Zappos' hiring strategy, weirdness can be defined as entrepreneurial creativity...” Kim defines weirdness within an entrepreneurial setting as “an individual difference characterized by failing to adhere to widely accepted social norms regarding one's appearance, speech, or behavior, such that one is considered odd, strange, or abnormal.”

Of course, a voluntary adoption of eccentricity can be guaranteed to attract attention, which is certainly a fundamental requirement for success. But one selectively takes on eccentricity at some peril, at least here in the United States.

As Kim more than hints, weirdness—the contemporary form of eccentricity—can be employed as a magic token for increasing one’s chances for success. But it also leads to a so far unanswered binary question: Is the person acting weirdly because he wants to be seen as special, gifted, and destined for storied success—perhaps the nation’s next trillionaire? Or, alternatively, does his eccentric weirdness, taken in its totality, suggest nothing more than that he is a very disturbed person indeed?

Richard M. Restak, M.D

item.title: "My Ex Is Crazy": True or False?
item.description:
Cognition

"My Ex Is Crazy": True or False?

A label ends the question. That is exactly what makes it feel like an answer.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Under uncertainty, a settled answer can feel better than a fuller one.
  • Some psychology-sounding words are diagnoses. Most are not.
  • An agreeable chatbot can make a one-sided account feel like a verdict.

It was a Monday in March, or that is how I remember it. I was 18, in a small mountain town, finishing a two-page letter to my first girlfriend about why I was ending it. Handwritten, because that is what you did. The reasons were ordinary, and I believe they were true. We wanted different things. We reacted badly to each other. Neither of us was going to give way.

It took two pages because I was trying to be fair to her.

Then, folding it, another thought arrived. What if none of this was ours? What if she was ill?

I did not put it in the letter. I remember the relief of it, though, and the thought has never entirely left.

The letter took two pages. The shortcut took a sentence.

And the shortcut did not replace the two pages. It offered to explain them all at once.

That is the part worth looking at. Relational reasoning is slow and stays uncomfortable because it keeps both people in the frame. A diagnostic label is fast and feels complete. It moves the cause out of the space between two people and lodges it inside one of them, where it can be filed. Relationships are seldom true or false.

Psychologists call this pull the need for cognitive closure: the desire for a definite answer when ambiguity is hard to bear. Under uncertainty we may seize on early information, and once a judgment has formed we become less willing to reopen it. A breakup creates exactly those conditions. The ambiguity is high, the cost of sitting in it is real, and no one will ever adjudicate what happened.

Memory does not hold the line either. In one study, people rated their dating partners, then two months later rated them again and tried to recall their original ratings. Those whose impressions had improved remembered their earlier evaluations as warmer than they had ac18tually been. Those whose impressions had soured remembered them as colder. Once a verdict is in, the record starts agreeing with it.

What has changed since that Monday is not the reflex. It is the supply.

At 18, the thought had nowhere to go. There was no search box in that room. The people I could have said it to knew one or both of us and might have pushed back. Now it has somewhere to go within seconds. Couples therapists report hearing the same vocabulary: narcissist, borderline, bipolar, avoidant. Around it sit terms for conduct or relationship dynamics: gaslighting, love-bombing, trauma bond.

These words do not have the same status. Narcissistic and borderline personality disorders and bipolar disorder are diagnoses. Avoidant attachment is not; nor are the last three. All can name something real. The trouble begins when a word settles a history before it has explained it.

Search any of them next to partner or ex and the checklists appear, built around signs to recognize rather than evidence that would rule the label out.

article continues after advertisement

An agreeable chatbot can go further. It works inside the account you give it, which you have already shaped, already sorted, already stripped of the parts that cut the other way, and it can hand that account back cleaner and more settled than you supplied it. In April 2025, OpenAI rolled back a version of its model after it became markedly more agreeable; the company later described it as validating doubts and reinforcing negative emotions in ways it had not intended. Whatever comes back, the account still has one witness.

I want to be careful here. Some partners do meet diagnostic criteria. Some people have been gaslit or otherwise abused, and finding the accurate word can be where clarity begins. My question is narrower: What happens when the word arrives as a verdict before the evidence has earned it?

Is this an explanation—or the end of one?

I use three checks to slow a verdict I already hold.

  • Date the word. When did it first occur to me, and how had I described the same events before it did?

  • Rewrite one episode in verbs. What was said and done, in order, with no character labels. Some episodes get more serious in translation. Others lose most of their force. Either result tells you something.

  • Then ask what the label made unnecessary: what was happening between us, what else was going on around us, and what my own part in it was.
